Your share award’s headline value is not yet spending cash: draw the vesting schedule

Compare hypothetical cliff and gradual vesting, split gross value into vested and unvested parts, reconcile the total and test different service milestones in four charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate an award’s units, vesting percentage and gross notional value

Interactive planning lab

Whole award at the entered price · gross notional value$30,000
Cliff schedule · gross value of vested units$0
Gradual schedule · gross value of vested units$12,000

One original hypothetical share-linked award, with alternative service-only vesting schedules applied to the same units. “Cliff” means none until the selected whole-year milestone, then all; “gradual” means equal portions after each completed year until full vesting. No partial-year service, monthly vesting, performance hurdles, new grants, dividends, acceleration, replacement awards or actual plan terms are included. A single independent CAD share-price assumption values all units and scenarios; it is not a price quote, stock forecast, accounting grant-date fair value or guaranteed payment. No shares are sold and no cash is credited. All amounts are gross, before tax, withholding and dealing costs. Vesting does not establish delivery timing, permission to sell or spendable proceeds. Fractional units are retained mathematically; actual award rounding is not modeled.

The central idea

The number of units, the vested fraction, the price used for valuation and the date cash becomes usable are separate parts of an equity-compensation plan.

01

Identify what was granted before valuing the number on screen

A compensation statement may show an attractive total for a share-linked award. The figure alone does not establish how much has vested, what will be delivered or when proceeds can fund a household payment.

FINRA’s questions about stock awards distinguishes employee options, restricted stock units and other equity arrangements, and explains why time and performance conditions matter. An option’s exercise right and an RSU-style unit are different instruments. This calculator uses a simplified share-linked unit, without an exercise price.

The example is independent of any employer plan. It compares two explicitly invented service schedules applied to one award. The amounts are expressed in CAD solely as the example’s valuation currency; the schedules are not a statement of Canadian or U.S. minimum vesting rules.

02

Write the two service rules before plotting them

The original award contains 600 units. Each is valued using an independent CAD 50 share-price assumption, giving a whole-award gross notional value of CAD 30,000. The selected comparison date is after two completed service years.

Under the default cliff rule, no units vest until three whole service years have been completed, at which point all 600 vest. Under the default gradual rule, one-fifth of the original award vests after each completed year, reaching full vesting after five years.

The step chart makes both rules visible. It does not spread a cliff award evenly across the preceding years or assume partial-year service qualifies. An actual agreement may count dates, hours or performance milestones differently; replace the simplified exercise with the confirmed schedule before evaluating a real award.

03

The same CAD 30,000 total can contain very different rights

At year two, the three-year cliff has not been reached, so the cliff example has zero vested units. All 600 remain unvested, with CAD 30,000 of gross notional value at the entered price.

The gradual example has vested two-fifths of 600, or 240 units. At CAD 50 each, their gross notional value is CAD 12,000. The remaining 360 units have CAD 18,000 of gross notional value and remain unvested.

The stacked bars have the same CAD 30,000 total because the award size and valuation price match. Reading only the total would conceal the different composition. Adding CAD 30,000 and CAD 12,000 as separate household assets would count the vested portion twice.

04

A gradual schedule is not ahead at every service date

Change completed service to three years. The default cliff rule now vests all 600 units, with CAD 30,000 of gross value at the entered price. The five-year gradual rule vests only three-fifths, or 360 units, with CAD 18,000 of gross value.

The ordering has reversed from the year-two comparison. At five completed years, both schedules have vested all units and their classified values coincide. The earlier advantage of a gradual schedule does not make it superior at every date.

This comparison isolates vesting mechanics while holding the grant and price fixed. It does not compare salaries, future awards, job satisfaction, employment risk or the value of another offer. A single upcoming milestone is one input to a job-change plan, rather than a complete reason to stay or leave.

05

A vesting percentage and a share price change different quantities

Keep the default two-year service date and reduce the valuation price from CAD 50 to CAD 30. The gradual schedule still vests 40% of the award and still corresponds to 240 vested units. Their gross notional value falls from CAD 12,000 to CAD 7,200.

The whole award’s value falls from CAD 30,000 to CAD 18,000. Its unvested portion falls from CAD 18,000 to CAD 10,800. All dollar values scale with the chosen price, while the number of units and vested fractions remain unchanged.

The price input is a stress assumption, not a forecast of what the employer’s stock will trade at on a future date. The matrix uses the same fixed price across its dates to isolate schedule differences. It does not imply that the stock price will remain constant over time.

06

Reconcile gross vested value without inventing a cash transaction

For the gradual schedule at year two, the waterfall begins with the whole-award CAD 30,000 gross value and subtracts CAD 18,000 associated with unvested units. The endpoint is CAD 12,000 associated with vested units.

This is a classification bridge. It does not mean CAD 30,000 entered a bank account and CAD 18,000 was then charged as a penalty. No sale, delivery or cash receipt occurs in the model. A potential forfeiture must be evaluated from the actual award’s termination and other provisions.

The computation retains fractional units where a chosen award size does not divide evenly into the chosen annual portions. That preserves the stated percentage calculation. Actual rounding, whole-share delivery or cash-in-lieu treatment can differ and must come from the award terms.

07

Vesting, delivery and usable cash need separate dates

The U.S. Office of Government Ethics’ RSU definition distinguishes the grant from the later stock or cash distribution and notes that distribution may be deferred under some plans. It is cited here for that instrument distinction, rather than for anyone’s disclosure obligations.

Even when an actual award vests, the household still needs to confirm what is delivered, its settlement date, any withholding and whether a sale is permitted. The gross notional value of vested units is therefore not automatically the amount that can be spent.

This calculator includes no tax calculation, payroll withholding, sale costs, trading restriction or currency conversion. It also adds no new grants, dividends or dividend equivalents. Entering a higher price cannot resolve those separate questions or supply cash before it is actually usable.

08

Use the matrix to expose a milestone assumption

The matrix changes completed service years and the number of years over which equal annual portions fully vest. Each cell values the remaining unvested units using the same award size and entered price. The cliff milestone does not enter this gradual-only comparison.

A zero cell means all units have vested under that mathematical schedule. It does not establish that shares were delivered, that a sale can settle in time or that the proceeds will cover a goal. A positive cell is the gross value still attached to unvested units, rather than a probability-weighted loss.

  1. Confirm the award type and original unit count.
  2. Read each vesting milestone and the service or performance conditions.
  3. Check what happens under the relevant departure circumstances.
  4. Record delivery, withholding and permitted-sale timing separately.
  5. Count only independently verified usable cash against an immediate payment.

Employer-linked compensation can also concentrate job income and investment exposure in the same company. The separate employer-concentration article tests that joint risk using existing vested, saleable holdings. Keep contingent awards distinct when connecting the two exercises.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All four charts are original hypothetical service-only award calculations. No actual employer, grant, employee account, market price, tax rate or vesting entitlement is used. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FINRA · Questions Employees Should Ask About Stock Awards ↗

    Published 25 October 2024; reviewed 25 October 2026. General distinctions among award types, time and performance vesting, concentration and tax questions. The two service schedules, original award and CAD valuation here are independent hypothetical assumptions, not a FINRA-recommended plan or an actual employer’s terms.

  2. U.S. Office of Government Ethics · Definitions · Restricted Stock Unit ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for the distinction between an RSU grant, vesting and distribution, including possible deferred delivery. Used only for instrument terminology. No public-official reporting requirement, employment right or national tax treatment is determined by this article.
